readingInstruction: Read Song of Solomon 1:1-4:16. This is a love poem between a man and a woman. Read it slowly, as poetry. Do not rush to allegory or avoid it as embarrassing. First, let it be what it is.
settingTheScene: The Song of Songs, “which is Solomon’s,” means “the best song.” It is a collection of love poems in dialogue between a bride, a bridegroom, and a chorus of friends, the “daughters of Jerusalem.” It celebrates erotic love within marriage. It is placed here because the wisdom books explore how to live well in God’s world, and a good marriage is one of the central gifts. The song has also been read throughout church history as a picture of Christ’s love for his people.
observation: “Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth! For your love is better than wine” (1:2).
“I am black and lovely, O daughters of Jerusalem” (1:5).
“As a lily among brambles, so is my love among the young women” (2:2).
“He brought me to the banqueting house, and his banner over me was love” (2:4).
“My beloved is mine, and I am his” (2:16).
“I adjure you, O daughters of Jerusalem… that you not stir up or awaken love until it pleases” (2:7).
“You are altogether beautiful, my love; there is no flaw in you” (4:7).
“A garden locked is my sister, my bride, a spring locked, a fountain sealed” (4:12).
interpretation:
The Song begins with desire. The woman speaks first, and her words are bold. She longs for her beloved’s kisses. The Bible does not shy away from the physical side of love. The Song presents it as a good gift of God, to be celebrated within the covenant of marriage. In a world that treats sex either as shameful or as trivial, the Song says it is beautiful and holy.

The couple exchange compliments in rich poetic images that can sound strange to modern ears: eyes like doves, hair like a flock of goats, a nose like a tower of Lebanon. These were images of beauty and delight in the ancient world. The man praises the woman’s beauty, and the woman praises his. They value each other. The mutuality is striking.

The refrain of 2:7, “Do not stir up or awaken love until it pleases,” appears three times in the Song. It is a warning to the daughters of Jerusalem: love should not be forced or rushed. It has a time. This is a wise word for a culture that hurries into physical intimacy. Love is powerful, and it should be treated with care.

In chapter 2, the poem moves to spring. “For behold, the winter is past; the rain is over and gone. The flowers appear on the earth.” Love is like the renewal of the earth. There are scenes of longing and search, of delight in the other’s presence. The woman says, “My beloved is mine, and I am his.” It is a statement of covenant belonging.

Chapter 3 includes a dream or search at night and the wedding procession of Solomon. Chapter 4 is the groom’s long praise of his bride on their wedding night. The garden imagery, “a garden locked,” speaks of purity and exclusivity. And the bride’s response is an invitation: “Let my beloved come to his garden, and eat its choicest fruits.” Love is both reserved and freely given.
connection: Christian readers have long seen in the Song a picture of Christ and his church. Ephesians 5:25-32 calls marriage a profound mystery pointing to Christ and the church. John 3:29 says, “The one who has the bride is the bridegroom.” Revelation 19:7 describes the marriage of the Lamb. At the same time, the Song stands as a celebration of human marriage in its own right. Jesus affirmed marriage as God’s design from the beginning (Matthew 19:4-6).
application:
If you are married, speak words of praise to your spouse today.

If you are single, thank God for the gift of marriage as a picture of Christ’s love.

Ask God to help you honor desire in the right time and place.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for love and for the picture of Christ and his church in marriage.
Ask him to teach you to value what he has given in its proper time.
Pray for those who are lonely or married, as it fits.
